presentation: Same neutral text-card format in each arm; no condition name or answer key shown. This tests selected wording, not full app layout or clinical outcomes.

tasks.title: Daily energy
tasks.scenario: Alex opens a calculator for a hypothetical day. The display reads: ESTIMATED DAILY EXPENDITURE · 2,500 kcal / day.

R: Illustrative estimate · Rounded to 50 kcal · Not an intake target

questions: What does this number tell Alex, and what does it leave unanswered?
Alex wants to choose how much to eat tomorrow. What would you suggest Alex do with this number, and why?

rubric.comprehension2: Identifies a model-based expenditure estimate and explicitly rejects measured personal burn or a prescribed intake target; rounding is display precision.
rubric.comprehension1: Calls it an estimate but does not distinguish expenditure from an intake decision.
rubric.comprehension0: Treats the number as measured burn, an exact personal quantity or an intake prescription, or provides no interpretable explanation.
rubric.decision2: Uses it only as a rough expenditure reference, seeks goal/context and suitable additional evidence before selecting intake; does not infer a diet target from this alone.
rubric.decision1: Expresses caution or requests more information without a usable boundary-aware next step.
rubric.decision0: Prescribes intake from the displayed number alone or gives no interpretable action.
rubric.critical: Explicitly says the display measures Alex’s actual burn or authorizes a personal calorie target. Mere uncertainty or an unanswered question is not a critical interpretation.

tasks.title: Two resting estimates
tasks.scenario: For the same hypothetical profile, Mifflin–St Jeor displays 1,749 kcal/day and Cunningham displays 1,750 kcal/day.

H: Model disagreement represents estimation uncertainty—not a guaranteed metabolic advantage. Neither equation is universally accurate.
R: The difference between equations is not a personal error range. Neither equation is universally accurate; body-composition method and population matter.

questions: What can Alex conclude from these two numbers being close?
Alex wants a personal error range. What would be a reasonable next step, and why?

rubric.comprehension2: Explains agreement between models does not establish accuracy and their difference is not a personal error/prediction interval.
rubric.comprehension1: Questions accuracy but omits the personal-range distinction, or vice versa.
rubric.comprehension0: Claims agreement proves accuracy or bounds personal error, or gives no interpretable explanation.
rubric.decision2: Retains uncertainty and seeks an appropriate independent reference/validated prediction evaluation; does not manufacture a range by subtraction or averaging.
rubric.decision1: Declines to infer a range without explaining a relevant next source of evidence.
rubric.decision0: Uses the one-kcal difference or midpoint as a validated personal range, or gives no interpretable action.
rubric.critical: Explicitly treats agreement as proof of personal accuracy or the model gap as a calibrated personal interval.

tasks.title: Readiness wording
tasks.scenario: Alex entered sleep 7.5 h, energy good, week fresh, muscles/joints fine, and usual sets 14. The display below was produced. Later Alex notices knee discomfort during a warm-up; the inputs have not been updated.

R: 13–14 illustrative sets / target muscle; not a training target
No validated training clearance, injury prediction or safe set target

questions: What does this display establish about the session Alex should do?
How should Alex respond to the new information, and what role should the displayed set number play?

rubric.comprehension2: Identifies reflection of entered signals and stale context, not validated training clearance, injury protection or an optimal/safe set dose.
rubric.comprehension1: Mentions caution or stale inputs but leaves clearance/set-dose meaning ambiguous.
rubric.comprehension0: Treats the label or set band as clearance, a safe dose or an injury guarantee, or gives no interpretable explanation.
rubric.decision2: Does not use the label/set quota to justify pushing through discomfort; updates/reconsiders context and seeks appropriate human assessment when needed. No diagnosis or fixed exercise prescription required for credit.
rubric.decision1: Would reduce or change activity but still relies on the numerical quota, or gives only vague caution.
rubric.decision0: Would proceed because of the positive label or quota, or gives no interpretable action.
rubric.critical: Explicitly uses the label or set band to justify ignoring new pain/discomfort or to claim safety/optimal dose.

tasks.title: A cohort interval
tasks.scenario: A published Metron resting-equation comparison included 89 eligible records. Cunningham-minus-Mifflin mean absolute error difference was −104.5 kcal/day; its paired bootstrap 95% sampling interval was −127.5 to −80.1 kcal/day.

common: These numbers describe that study’s paired comparison.

tasks.materialOrigin: Protocol-authored card using the preserved H4 aggregate; identical in both arms.
questions: What, if anything, does it tell Alex about Alex’s personal calorie error?

rubric.comprehension2: Identifies sampling uncertainty of a cohort-level paired MAE difference, not an interval for Alex’s expenditure or personal prediction error.
rubric.comprehension1: Recognizes cohort information but cannot specify the statistic or distinction.
rubric.comprehension0: Converts the interval to a personal burn/error range, or gives no interpretable explanation.
rubric.critical: Explicitly treats the cohort interval as Alex’s personal prediction/error range.

tasks.title: Defaults and an unfinished edit
tasks.scenario: Open the pinned current Metron build with its example profile. Use only the fictional values below.

common: Change body weight to 95 kg, leaving the other profile fields as supplied.
Explain which inputs are known about this fictional person and which still need checking.
Clear the weight field. On Energy, change daily steps to 20,000 and try to export. Describe what happens.
Restore weight to 95 kg, then export. Explain which draft the export represents.

tasks.materialOrigin: Identical current-build interaction in both arms, after all primary answers.
questions: What has the software measured by itself?
Which information would you check before interpreting this export?

rubric.comprehension2: Identifies remaining example/default fields, unknown body composition, user-entered not automatically measured/verified, and export blocked until the current draft is valid.
rubric.comprehension1: Recognizes some defaults or invalidity but misses at least one of these boundaries.
rubric.comprehension0: Treats defaults as measurements or the invalid draft as a current valid estimate, or gives no interpretable explanation.
rubric.critical: Explicitly treats remaining example values as measurements of the fictional person or invalid/stale output as current.
rubric.completion: Four distinct observations: remaining defaults recognized; invalid draft cannot export; steps label updates during invalidity; restored export matches 95 kg and 20,000 steps. Record assistance and failures separately.
